title: Overlord (2018): Watch J.J. Abrams' WWII Horror Free on Tubi
subtitle: They were supposed to blow up a radio tower. Then they found what was in the basement.
intro: D-Day minus one. A small American unit drops behind enemy lines in occupied France with a clean mission: destroy a German communications tower before the invasion begins. They find the tower. They also find something underneath it that has no place in any war film you've ever seen. Overlord is a WWII movie that earns its action credentials in the first twenty minutes and then quietly kicks the door open on something much worse. It is not subtle about what it becomes. It doesn't need to be.

items.name: Jovan Adepo
items.bio: Adepo plays Boyce, a young private who is too decent for what this mission asks of him. He's the audience's way in, the one soldier who hasn't made peace with the worst outcomes. When he finds what the Germans have been doing underground, he doesn't harden. He panics. That's the right call.

items.name: Wyatt Russell
items.bio: Russell plays Ford, the unit's hard-edged sergeant who has one priority: complete the mission, nothing else. He's not a villain. He's just a man who has decided the objective matters more than the horror. Every time Boyce wants to stop and process, Ford is already moving.

items.name: Pilou Asbæk
items.bio: Asbæk plays Wafner, the SS commander running the village and the experiments beneath it. He's not a cartoon. He's comfortable with power, and that comfort is what makes him frightening. There's a scene early on where he makes a decision about a civilian that tells you exactly who he is.

items.name: Mathilde Ollivier
items.bio: Ollivier plays Chloe, a French local who has been surviving under occupation through sheer calculation. She knows more than she says and says more than she should. She's the film's moral center in a story that keeps testing what moral center even means under those conditions.

quote: We have a mission. Whatever this is, it is not the mission.

whyWatch.body: Overlord commits to being two different films and refuses to apologize for either of them. The first act is a genuine WWII action film, the plane sequence alone is the kind of practical chaos that big-budget productions spend years trying to manufacture. By the time the horror arrives, you've already bought into the stakes. That sequencing is the whole game. You're not watching a genre gimmick. You're watching soldiers who signed up for one kind of danger get handed a completely different kind.
